pa-01.title: Government and Administration: What Are Public Services?
explain: **Public administration** is the activity through which government and public agencies actually carry out, in accordance with law and budgets, the work society needs. **The study of public administration** examines through what organizations and procedures, and according to what standards, that work is done. The countries, cities, and agencies in this course are all fictional.

Among the things government does, the ones that touch citizens' daily lives directly are **public services**. Paving roads, putting out fires, collecting garbage, and running school lunches are examples. Most of the money spent on public services comes from the **taxes** citizens pay.

Why does government take on this work? One reason is the nature of a **public good**. Something like a street lamp, which one person's use does not prevent others from using and whose users are hard to single out, is difficult to sell in a market for a price. So it is often provided jointly through taxes. Still, which services government provides directly and which it leaves to the private sector differs by country and era, and people disagree about it.

Administration is close to politics but not the same. Elected officials and the legislature set the broad direction, and administrative agencies carry out those decisions in line with law and procedure. Citizens pay taxes and receive services, and when something is inconvenient they send it back as opinions and complaints. The figure shows this cycle.

pa-02.title: The Policy Process: From Problem to Evaluation
explain: A **policy** is a course of action set by government, together with the means that follow from it, for solving a social problem or reaching a goal. The flow in which a policy is made and carried out is usually divided into five stages.

1. **Agenda setting**: the stage in which, among many problems, one rises to become a problem government should address.
2. **Policy formulation**: the stage in which alternatives for solving the problem are developed and compared.
3. **Policy decision**: the stage in which one of the alternatives is formally chosen.
4. **Policy implementation**: the stage in which an administrative agency actually carries out the chosen policy.
5. **Policy evaluation**: the stage in which one examines what results the policy produced.

The result of an evaluation is not an end but a new starting point. If the policy worked well it continues; if it fell short it is revised, or raised again onto the agenda as a new problem. This return of evaluation results to earlier stages is called **feedback**.

These five stages are a framework for understanding. In reality the stages sometimes overlap, and alternatives may be chosen again during implementation. It would be wrong to assume that every policy proceeds in a straight line in this order.

body: In the fictional city of Naru, several residents said it is uncomfortable to stand at a bus stop on rainy days. When this rises as a problem for city government to address, that is **agenda setting**. Comparing alternatives such as installing a roof, installing seats, or adjusting the interval between buses is **policy formulation**. When the mayor and the council settle on installing a roof, that is the **policy decision**, and choosing a contractor and putting up the roofs is **implementation**. Checking one year later, through a user survey, whether the discomfort has decreased is **evaluation**, and if shortcomings show up, the matter goes back to the agenda.

pa-03.title: Organizations: Bureaucracy and Structure
explain: Administration is not done alone; it is done through organizations. The representative form of a government organization is the **bureaucracy**. A bureaucracy is a way of organizing in which work is divided, lines of responsibility run up and down, and the organization operates by rules and documents.

The characteristics of a bureaucracy are summarized as follows.
- **Division of labor**: work is divided into departments and jobs.
- **Hierarchy**: there are lines of command and reporting running up and down.
- **Rules and documents**: people work according to set regulations and records.
- **Expertise**: people are assigned to jobs according to ability suited to the job.

The advantage of this approach is that, whoever handles a matter, it is processed by similar standards, so it is consistent and predictable, and it reduces differences in treatment from person to person. The disadvantage is that it easily becomes slow and inflexible because it is bound by rules, and **formalism**, in which following the rules becomes an end in itself, can arise.

The shape of an organization can also be chosen. A **hierarchical structure** has many layers, so instructions are clear, but information takes time to travel up and down. A **flat structure** has few layers, so communication is fast, but responsibility can become blurred or the range one person handles can become wide. One cannot say in a word which is better; it depends on the nature of the work.

pa-04.title: The Budget: Revenue and Expenditure
explain: A **budget** is a plan, set in advance, of how much government will collect and where it will spend it over a given period (usually one year). Because a policy is hard to carry out without a budget, a budget is sometimes read as a set of numbers showing what government considers important.

**Revenue** includes taxes paid by citizens and firms, grants the central government passes down to localities, and other income such as user fees. **Expenditure** includes project costs by field, such as welfare, transportation, and education. Comparing revenue with expenditure, when revenue is larger it is a **surplus**, and when expenditure is larger it is a **deficit**.

When a deficit arises, the question is how to cover the shortfall. There are ways of collecting more taxes, of cutting spending, and of borrowing money. Each puts the burden on different people at different times, so opinions differ about which is better depending on circumstances and values. This lesson does not decide which method is right; it learns how to calculate.

A budget usually moves through a cycle of formulation, deliberation and approval, execution, and settlement of accounts. An administrative agency draws up the plan (formulation), the legislature reviews and approves it (deliberation and approval), the money is spent as set (execution), and afterward how it was actually spent is compiled and checked (settlement of accounts).

pa-05.title: Citizen Participation and Complaints
explain: In a democratic society, administration is accountable to citizens. The routes through which citizens convey opinions to the administration and influence it are called **citizen participation**. The most basic are elections and voting, but there are also several routes that reach the administration in ordinary times.

A **civil petition** (minwon) is a citizen's request to an administrative agency or notice of an inconvenience. Reporting a street lamp that has gone out, applying for a document to be issued, and submitting an opinion on a policy are all civil petitions. The agency assigns a received petition to a person in charge, and after handling it replies with the result. A processing deadline is often set.

Besides petitions, there are various ways of participating.
- **Resident survey**: gathers the opinions of many people. It is simple but makes in-depth discussion difficult.
- **Public hearing**: concerned people gather and state their views. It has depth, but attendance is limited.
- **Participatory budgeting**: residents themselves propose and decide how part of the budget is used.
- **Citizen petition**: a certain number of people jointly submit a written request.

Participation always involves a question of balance. The more people participate, the higher the representativeness but the harder in-depth discussion becomes, and when a few discuss deeply, the question is whether their views represent the whole. There is also the problem that only people with time and leisure end up participating.

pa-06.title: Policy Evaluation: Effectiveness, Efficiency, and Equity
explain: Policy evaluation is the work of weighing what results a policy produced. Three criteria are commonly used in evaluation.

- **Effectiveness**: how far the goal was achieved. The number of people helped relative to the target number is an example.
- **Efficiency**: how large the outcome is relative to the resources put in. The cost of helping one person is an example.
- **Equity**: whether benefits and burdens were divided fairly. It looks at which regions or groups were left out.

The three criteria can pull in different directions. The route that helps many people at low cost (efficiency) may be one that leaves out outlying residents who are hard to reach. Which criterion to weigh more heavily is not decided by numbers but requires a value judgment, and different people can reach different conclusions from the same data.
So an evaluator should state the criteria first, show what data were used, and also say that conclusions may differ depending on the criteria.

pa-07.title: Policy Typology: Lowi's Classification and Wilson's Cost-Benefit Model
explain: Suppose Naru wants to pave a village road, tighten emissions standards for factories, and expand living support for low-income households. All are work done by the same city hall, yet the reactions of the city council, the press, and stakeholders are completely different. Road paving passes quietly, while emissions standards provoke months of argument. If policies are sorted by their content, could such differences be anticipated in advance? **Policy typology** grew out of this question. Lowi represents this approach with the proposition that "policy determines politics." The meaning is that politics does not make policy; rather, the character of a policy determines what kind of politics will unfold.

Lowi divided policies into four types according to the way government uses coercion.
- **Distributive policy**: hands out services and benefits to particular individuals or groups. The funding is borne jointly, so winners and losers are not clear-cut, and bargaining in which each side recognizes the other's share (logrolling) tends to occur. Examples: paving a village road, subsidies for local projects.
- **Regulatory policy**: restricts the conduct of individuals or groups or imposes obligations on them. Those regulated and those protected split, so conflict is great. Examples: emissions standards, limits on business hours.
- **Redistributive policy**: moves resources such as income or wealth from one group to another. Ideological conflict between classes tends to grow. Examples: progressive taxation and support for low-income groups.
- **Constituent policy**: sets the rules for creating and operating government bodies. Examples: the number of legislators and electoral districts, the pay system for civil servants.

Lowi's classification is simple because it rests on policy content, but in practice many policies mix several types. Wilson looked at the same problem from a different angle. He asks whether the **costs** and **benefits** produced by a policy are concentrated on a few or dispersed among many. The concentrated side has a large stake, so it forms organizations and acts actively, while the dispersed side finds it hard to organize because each individual gains or loses only a small share. Combining these two criteria yields the four types of politics shown in the figure.

explain.alt: A table with 2 rows and 2 columns. The column headings are "concentrated costs" and "dispersed costs," and the row headings are "concentrated benefits" and "dispersed benefits." The cell for concentrated benefits and concentrated costs reads "interest group politics, both sides organized and confronting each other"; concentrated benefits and dispersed costs reads "client politics, led by the beneficiary group"; dispersed benefits and concentrated costs reads "entrepreneurial politics, a policy entrepreneur is needed"; and dispersed benefits and dispersed costs reads "majoritarian politics, organized pressure is weak."
explain.caption: Wilson's four types of politics

explain: The knack for reading the figure is to ask "who moves?" In **interest group politics**, both those who gain the benefits and those who bear the costs are few and organized, so they confront each other head-on. In **client politics**, benefits are concentrated on a few while costs are spread widely, so the beneficiary group can easily drive the policy forward quietly. In **entrepreneurial politics**, a few bear the costs while the benefits are spread among many, so if left alone those bearing the costs oppose it while those gaining the benefits stay quiet. For such a policy to pass, an accident, an event, or a **policy entrepreneur** such as a civic group must make the dispersed interests visible. In **majoritarian politics**, both costs and benefits are widely spread, so organized pressure is weak.

The two theories answer different questions. Lowi predicts the shape of politics using the question "what kind of coercion does government use?", while Wilson predicts the organizability of opposition and support using the question "how are costs and benefits spread, and among whom?" In practice, Wilson's model is convenient when working out who the opposition will be and how to gather supporters.

The limits are also clear. A single policy can be both regulatory and redistributive in character, so the boundaries between types overlap. Because "concentrated" and "dispersed" in Wilson's model are not objective figures but degrees that people **perceive**, a major event can change the type of the same policy. Also, classifying the type is only a starting point for prediction, and actual outcomes also depend on other factors such as parties, public opinion, and institutions.

Step 1: Ask what each plan has government do. (A) hands out benefits, (B) restricts conduct, (C) moves resources from one group to another, and (D) sets the rules for how government is composed.
Step 2: (A) is distributive policy, (B) is regulatory policy, (C) is redistributive policy, and (D) is constituent policy.
Interpretation: Even among plans in the same city, we can predict that (B) and (C) tend to produce greater conflict, while (A) tends to pass relatively quietly. This is, however, only a tendency.

body: Conditions (fictional): (A) Naru limits the number of taxi licenses. The 40 existing taxi operators protect their interests, and the citizens as a whole pay slightly higher fares. (B) Three factories that discharge harmful substances into a river are required to install purification equipment. The factories bear large costs, and tens of thousands of downstream residents become slightly safer.

Step 1: In (A), the benefits are concentrated on a few operators and the costs are dispersed across all citizens. In (B), the costs are concentrated on a few factories and the benefits are dispersed among many residents.
Step 2: (A) is client politics and (B) is entrepreneurial politics.

Interpretation: In (A), the operators' associations act actively while opposition is scattered, so the status quo is easy to maintain. In (B), the factories oppose strongly, so passage is likely only when something makes the benefits visible, such as a major accident or the activity of a civic group.

pa-08.title: Policy Decision-Making Models: From the Rational Model to the Garbage Can Model
explain: Haedeun City Hall, trying to reduce traffic congestion, has dozens of alternatives: reorganizing bus routes, adjusting fares, widening roads, building bike lanes, and so on. How does a policymaker choose one of them? It would be simple to assume they compare all alternatives and choose the best, but in reality both information and time are lacking. The models of policy decision-making explain the distance between this ideal and reality in different ways.

The most basic is the **rational model**. It assumes a decision-maker with complete information and computational ability who decides in the following order.
1. Clearly define the problem and goals.
2. Find all possible alternatives.
3. Predict the consequences of each alternative.
4. Choose the alternative that best achieves the goals.

One way of comparing alternatives is the weighted sum. If the weight of evaluation criterion $i$ is $w_i$ (summing to 1) and the score alternative $j$ receives on criterion $i$ is $s_{ij}$, the overall score is $V_j = \sum_i w_i \cdot s_{ij}$. The alternative with the largest $V_j$ is the rational model's choice. Which criteria to include and what weights to give them is a value judgment, not a calculation. Even the same score table can lead to a different conclusion if the weights are changed.

Simon proposed the **satisficing model** on the grounds that human computational ability is limited. The decision-maker stops searching at the moment they find not the best alternative but one that feels "good enough." This is called bounded rationality. Lindblom's **incrementalist model** goes a step further, holding that the decision-maker compares a small number of alternatives that differ only slightly from the current policy and gains agreement through bargaining with stakeholders. This approach is politically feasible and carries little risk of failure. In return, it is criticized for carrying on the problems the existing policy already has, and for having difficulty responding to crises that require major change.

Etzioni's **mixed-scanning model** blends the two models. It scans broadly, as in the rational model, for fundamental direction, and treats detailed decisions narrowly, as in the incrementalist model. Cohen, March, and Olsen's **garbage can model** deals with organizations whose goals are unclear, whose participants come and go, and whose technology is uncertain. In such organizations, problems, solutions, participants, and choice opportunities each drift about, and a decision is made when they happen to meet in one place. Its distinctive point is that a decision may be the result of a chance meeting rather than a logical process of solving a problem.

The models are not copies of reality but frameworks that highlight certain aspects of it. Ordinary budget decisions are close to incremental, large projects started from scratch demand more rational analysis, and in chaotic organizations the garbage can appears. Even within a single policy decision, a different model may fit better at different stages, so rather than choosing which model is right, it is better to ask under what conditions each model has greater explanatory power.

examples.title: The weighted sum of the rational model
body: Conditions (fictional): Naru compares three village bus route plans. The criteria and weights are user convenience 0.5, cost savings 0.3, and equity 0.2. The scores (out of 10) are 8, 4, 6 for Plan A, 6, 9, 5 for Plan B, and 7, 7, 9 for Plan C.
Step 2: C $= 3.5 + 2.1 + 1.8 = 7.4$. The rational model chooses Plan C, the largest.

Interpretation: If the weights are changed to user convenience 0.2, cost savings 0.6, and equity 0.2, B becomes the largest at $1.2 + 5.4 + 1.0 = 7.6$. The conclusion depends not only on the scores but also on the weights.

examples.title: Incremental budget decisions
body: Conditions (fictional): Haedeun City's library had a budget of 8 billion won last year. The responsible department requested 9.2 billion won this year, and by custom the city council has adjusted within about 5% of the previous year.
Step 1: Take the previous year's budget as the baseline. A 5% increase over the baseline is $80 \times 1.05 = 84$ (in units of 100 million won, that is, 8.4 billion won).
Step 2: Negotiation takes place between 8 billion won and 9.2 billion won, but the actual agreement is likely to come within a narrow range around 8.4 billion won.

Interpretation: Rather than reviewing the structure of new projects from scratch, it makes small adjustments to the current one. It is politically stable, but does not ask whether the 8 billion won itself is appropriate.

Satisficing model

Incrementalist model
Emphasizes bargaining and adjustment that changes the current policy only slightly
Garbage can model

checks.explanation: A decision that changes only slightly from a baseline is the pattern of the incrementalist model.

In a crisis requiring drastic change, the problems of the existing policy may persist

pa-09.title: Policy Implementation and Evaluation Design: Street-Level Bureaucracy and Difference-in-Differences
explain: A policy being decided is not the end. It is common for service counters or welfare consultation offices that received the same guidelines to work differently from region to region. The policy changes in the course of implementation. And even if indicators improved after a program, whether it was thanks to the program has to be examined separately. This lesson deals with why implementation varies, and how effects are checked through design.

There are broadly two ways of looking at implementation. The **top-down approach** holds that implementation goes well when higher-level policy goals are clear and the implementation structure is well built. Statutes and guidelines, resources, and supervision are central. The **bottom-up approach** starts from the actions and interactions of implementers in the field. It examines who the people who actually make policy in the field are and under what constraints they work. The two approaches are less mutually exclusive than views of the same object from above and from below.

Lipsky's (1980) **street-level bureaucracy** is the representative bottom-up approach. Street-level bureaucrats are civil servants such as teachers, police officers, welfare caseworkers, and service counter staff, who meet citizens directly and hold considerable discretion. They always work with heavy workloads, scarce resources, and ambiguous goals. So coping methods arise to get through the work. They limit consultation time or ration service by queuing, fit complex cases into simple frameworks, and engage in **creaming**, choosing first the clients most likely to succeed. The key point is that this is behavior arising from structure, not from individual laziness.

Now let us move on to evaluation. If the recycling rate rose from 30% to 50% after a program, is the program's effect 20 percentage points? We cannot tell. It might have risen even without the program. An effect is the difference between "the case with the program" and "the case without it," and the latter cannot be observed (the counterfactual). So a comparison group is used to approximate it. Whether the comparison is trustworthy is judged by **internal validity**, that is, the degree to which a change in the outcome can be attributed to the program. Typical threats to it are external events in the same period (history), changes that arise on their own as time passes (maturation), differences between the treatment and comparison groups from the start (selection bias), and dropout (attrition).

**Difference-in-differences** (DID) is a simple design that uses a comparison group. From the treatment group's before-and-after change, subtract the comparison group's before-and-after change. $$\text{DID} = (Y_{\text{처치,후}} - Y_{\text{처치,전}}) - (Y_{\text{비교,후}} - Y_{\text{비교,전}})$$ (Reading the Korean labels: 처치 = treated, 비교 = comparison, 후 = post, 전 = pre.) The comparison group's change stands in for the change that would have occurred in both groups in common even without the program. In the figure, the dotted line is the value the treatment group would have reached had it moved in parallel with the comparison group.

explain.alt: A line graph with before and after the program on the horizontal axis and the recycling rate (20 to 60) on the vertical axis. The orange line (Naru, program implemented) rises from 30 to 50, and the green line (Haedeun, comparison) rises from 28 to 38. A gray dotted line starts from Naru's before-program value and rises in a direction parallel to the green line.
explain.caption: Change in the recycling rate in two cities

explain: For DID to hold, the **parallel trends** assumption is needed. It is the assumption that, without the program, the two groups' trends of change would have been the same. This assumption cannot be tested directly, and is checked indirectly by whether the trends at several points before the program were similar. The estimate also becomes unreliable when the comparison group is affected by the program (contamination) or when different external events hit the two groups. It should be remembered that DID is not a cure-all but a design with clear assumptions.

examples.title: A simple before-and-after comparison versus DID
body: Conditions (fictional): Naru ran a job-matching program. The employment rate in the treated area went from 40% to 55%, and over the same period in the comparison area from 41% to 50%.
Step 1: The simple change in the treated area is $55 - 40 = 15$ percentage points, and the change in the comparison area is $50 - 41 = 9$ percentage points.
Step 2: $\text{DID} = 15 - 9 = 6$ percentage points.

Interpretation: The estimate of the program's effect is 6 percentage points, not 15. The remaining 9 percentage points can be viewed as a change that occurred in common in both areas (the economy and so on). This holds, however, only on the condition that the parallel trends assumption is correct.

examples.title: Creaming and performance indicators
body: Conditions (fictional): A job-seeker counseling office's performance indicator is the job-placement rate (number of placements ÷ number of consultations). Originally it counseled 100 people and placed 50 (50%). One counselor counseled only 60 people with high chances of employment and placed 45.
Step 1: The new job-placement rate rose to $45 \div 60 = 75$%.
Step 2: However, the number of people counseled fell from 100 to 60, and 40 were left out of counseling.

Interpretation: The indicator improved, but users in difficult circumstances were excluded. Because indicators change behavior in the field, they must be designed with street-level bureaucrats' coping methods in mind.

checks.prompt: Match each concept with its explanation.
checks.hint: Separate the directions of looking at implementation from the threats to evaluation.
checks.explanation: The first two are approaches to looking at implementation, creaming is a street-level bureaucrat's coping response, and history is a threat to internal validity.

Emphasizes the clarity of higher-level policy goals and the implementation structure
Bottom-up approach
Starts from the discretion and interactions of field implementers
Creaming
Choosing clients most likely to succeed in order to meet a performance indicator

An external event occurring in the same period as the program affects the outcome

pa-10.title: Administrative Values and Weber's Bureaucracy
explain: At a service counter, is refusing to accept an application because one document is missing the right thing to do, or is it inflexibility? Handling things quickly and handling them accurately, listening to citizens' views and deciding fast, sometimes collide. The values concerning what administration should work for and by what standards are called **administrative values**. Rather than giving a single right answer, the study of public administration helps us understand the meanings of these values and the tensions among them.

The representative administrative values are as follows.
- **Legality**: administration is conducted according to statutes and procedures. It prevents arbitrary administration.
- **Efficiency**: how much output is produced relative to the resources put in. Beyond cost savings, there is also the concept of **social efficiency**, which takes human values into account.
- **Democracy**: guarantees citizen participation and responds to citizens' demands.
- **Equity**: divides benefits and burdens fairly and gives consideration to people in disadvantaged positions.
- **Effectiveness**: how far the set goals were achieved.
- **Accountability and transparency**: explaining and disclosing the process and results of administration.

Efficiency is the easiest to express numerically. $$\text{능률} = \frac{\text{산출}}{\text{투입}}$$ (That is, efficiency = output ÷ input; 능률 = efficiency, 산출 = output, 투입 = input.) For example, the number of petitions one staff member handles in a month is a simple efficiency indicator. But looking only at this number can lead to giving up carefulness in order to raise the number handled. We must always remember the risk that a value that is easy to express in numbers will push out other values.

Weber's **bureaucracy** ideal type is the form in which these values appear as a concrete organization. Its features include authority based on rules, hierarchical ranking, handling by documents, specialized division of labor, impersonality that is not swayed by emotion, and appointment by ability with career protection. Such a structure has people work similarly regardless of who is in charge and raises predictability and fairness. It can be seen as a design that pursues legality and efficiency together with a certain degree of equity.

At the same time, bureaucracy has dysfunctions. When rules and documents grow excessive, red tape arises; following rules becomes the aim and the original goal is forgotten, producing **goal displacement**; and trained incapacity is pointed out, in which people grow used to one way of doing things and cannot adapt to new situations. There is also the tension that the more strictly legality is observed, the less democracy (responsiveness) there is.

The priority among values differs by situation and by values held, and one cannot say that any one is always right. Also, Weber's ideal type is not a literal description of real organizations but a reference model built by extracting features for comparison and analysis. Real government organizations deviate from this model in various directions.

examples.title: The efficiency of two counters
body: Conditions (fictional): At Naru's service counter A, 4 staff members handle 1,200 cases a month; at counter B, 5 staff members handle 1,400 cases.
Step 1: A's cases per person are $1200 \div 4 = 300$.
Step 2: For B, $1400 \div 5 = 280$ cases.

Interpretation: Judging by the number of cases handled alone, A is more efficient. But if B has fewer repeat-visit requests or spends more time serving vulnerable groups, that does not show up in this indicator. An efficiency indicator must be read together with other values.

examples.title: Reading a clash of values
body: Conditions (fictional): A household hit by heavy rain applied for emergency assistance but was refused because it had no copy of its lease. The staff member followed the regulations.
Step 1: The staff member's behavior followed the regulations precisely and so fits legality.
Step 2: However, in that it failed to respond to the citizen's circumstances in an emergency, democracy and equity become issues.

Interpretation: This does not mean breaking the regulations. In emergencies, a procedure allowing documents to be supplemented later can be built into the regulations in advance, satisfying legality and responsiveness together.

checks.prompt: Match each administrative value with its explanation.
checks.hint: See what standard each value takes as its basis.
checks.explanation: Administrative values are standards of what administration should pursue, and they can be in tension with one another.

Administration is conducted according to statutes and procedures
Efficiency
Makes output large relative to the resources put in
Democracy
Responds to citizens' participation and demands
Equity
Divides benefits and burdens fairly and gives consideration to the weak

checks.prompt: Counter B added one staff member to reach 6, and its monthly caseload became 1,500. By how many cases did cases per person change from the example's 280? (negative if it decreased)
checks.hint: Find 1500 ÷ 6 and compare it with 280.
checks.explanation: 1500 ÷ 6 = 250, so 250 − 280 = −30 cases. If total cases do not rise in proportion when staff increases, efficiency per person falls.

checks.hint: See how the result of following the regulations worked on the citizen's circumstances.
checks.explanation: It is a scene in which legality, observing procedure, collides with responsiveness to urgent circumstances.

That efficiency and effectiveness coincide completely
That neither accountability nor transparency is important
The distinction between constituent policy and regulatory policy

checks.hint: Think about what the name ideal type means.
checks.explanation: An ideal type is a tool for analyzing reality, and real organizations deviate from this model.
options: It is a statement of fact that all real government organizations have these features exactly
It is a reference model built by extracting features for analysis and comparison, and reality differs from it
It is a claim that the more rules there are, the higher efficiency always becomes

pa-11.title: New Public Management (NPM): Introducing Market Principles and Their Limits
explain: In the 1970s and 1980s, public finances grew tight in many countries and dissatisfaction grew that government was big and inefficient. Traditional bureaucracy was criticized as strong at following rules but weak at taking responsibility for results. In response, a movement arose to bring business management methods and market principles into the public sector. This is called **New Public Management** (NPM).

NPM is less a single theory than a common tendency seen in reforms in several countries. The introduction of executive agencies in Britain (1988) and New Zealand's reforms are representative, and Osborne and Gaebler, in their 1992 book, spoke of an entrepreneurial government that "steers rather than rows." The idea is that government does not produce every service directly but sets the direction of policy, and production can be left to competing suppliers.

The core elements are summarized as follows.
- **Performance orientation**: manage and reward by results and performance indicators rather than inputs and rules.
- **Introducing competition**: create competition among suppliers through contracting out, bidding, and internal markets.
- **Customer orientation**: treat citizens as customers of services and raise their satisfaction.
- **Decentralization and autonomy**: reduce rules, give agency heads operating autonomy, and hold them accountable.

Representative tools include the **executive agency** (an agency whose executing function is separated out and whose head is given operating autonomy and responsibility for performance), **contracting out** (leaving service production to the private sector by contract), the **voucher** (giving users a coupon so they choose the supplier), and the **performance contract** (setting goals and indicators in advance and evaluating by the degree of attainment).

Whether contracting out really reduces costs has to be calculated. The total cost of contracting out includes, in addition to the contract price, the **management and oversight costs** of selecting suppliers, supervising them, and checking performance. It is a saving only when the in-house cost is greater than the total cost of contracting out. The harder a service is to supervise by contract, the larger this cost becomes.

NPM has also been criticized. If one prizes only what is captured by performance indicators, values that are hard to measure (equity, trust) get pushed aside, and behavior aimed at hitting the indicators (creaming, manipulating indicators) appears. It is also pointed out that seeing citizens only as customers obscures their status as citizens with rights and duties. When a problem arises in a contracted-out service, it can also become unclear who is responsible. Conversely, some assess that service quality or cost improved in certain areas, so the performance of NPM itself is debated depending on the country and field.

examples.title: Total cost of in-house versus contracting out
body: Conditions (fictional): Management of a municipal parking lot in Haedeun. The in-house cost is 12 eok won a year (1 eok = 100 million won). The private contract price is 10 eok won a year, and contract supervision and performance checks cost 1.5 eok won a year.
Step 1: The total cost of contracting out is $10 + 1.5 = 11.5$ eok won.
Step 2: Compared with in-house, $12 - 11.5 = 0.5$ eok won is saved, a savings rate of about 4.2%.

Interpretation: Looking at the contract price alone, the saving is 2 eok won, but including the oversight cost it shrinks to 0.5 eok won. If the oversight cost is 2.5 eok won, the total cost becomes 12.5 eok won, which is instead an increase of 0.5 eok won.

examples.title: Distortion of performance indicators
body: Conditions (fictional): Naru evaluates a cleaning contractor only by its "collection completion rate." The contractor put off collection in hard-to-reach alleys and worked mainly on the easy-to-collect main streets.
Step 1: Working mainly on main streets raises the completion rate in a short time.
Step 2: Alley residents suffer greater inconvenience, but it does not show in the indicator.
Interpretation: Performance-oriented management works only when the indicator properly represents the goal. Supplementary indicators, such as collection times by alley section, are needed.

checks.explanation: All four tools are NPM approaches that rely on results, competition, and autonomy.

pa-12.title: The New Public Service (NPS) and New Governance: How We See Citizens
explain: NPM saw citizens as customers and tried to make government an efficient service supplier. But is a user of public services the same as a shop's customer? Citizens are not merely people who receive services; they are also the owners who pay taxes, discuss policy, and decide matters of the community. Questions raised about this limit of NPM gave rise to new perspectives.

The Denhardts (Denhardt & Denhardt) proposed the **New Public Service** (NPS). Summarizing some of its principles: "serve citizens, not customers," "the public interest is not a by-product of individual interests but a goal created together through dialogue," "help citizens find common interests rather than steering," "accountability is not simple," and "value people, not just productivity." Government officials play the role not of entrepreneurs but of servants who protect public values.

**New governance** is yet another current. From the recognition that modern public problems (the environment, care, regional regeneration) are hard for government to solve alone, it refers to a way of solving problems in which government, the market, and civil society cooperate in networks. Government becomes a coordinator and participant rather than commanding through hierarchy, and draws out trust and cooperation. NPS and new governance have much in common but are not the same thing. NPS stresses the values of citizenship and the public interest, and new governance stresses a cooperative operating structure.

explain.alt: A table. The columns are New Public Management (NPM) and New Public Service (NPS). The citizen row reads "customer" and "citizen," the government role row reads "steering" and "serving," the core value row reads "efficiency and performance" and "public interest and democratic values," and the operating method row reads "competition and performance contracts" and "dialogue and joint shaping."
explain.caption: Comparing NPM and NPS

explain: The figure compares how NPM and NPS see the same administrative phenomenon differently. If citizens are seen as customers, satisfaction surveys and service improvement are central; if seen as citizens, deliberation, participation, and community building are central. The role of government also shifts from steering to serving. Even for the same park management, NPM would stress contract costs and user satisfaction, while NPS would stress the process of consulting residents and the agreement of the local community.

When the perspective differs, so do the criteria of evaluation. If programs are evaluated with weights such as efficiency 40%, citizen participation 30%, and equity 30%, it becomes $V = 0.4 \times \text{효율} + 0.3 \times \text{참여} + 0.3 \times \text{형평}$ (효율 = efficiency, 참여 = participation, 형평 = equity). The weights reveal which perspective is prized, and changing the weights can change the ranking. Which weights are right is not settled by calculation.

It is therefore not enough to see the two paradigms only as a question of superiority in which one replaces the other. For standardized services the tools of NPM fit well, and for matters requiring the agreement of the local community NPS may fit better. Within a single policy, the two are often mixed, such as using contracting out while setting up a residents' council. NPS is criticized as strongly normative and hard to measure in terms of performance, and NPM has the limits seen earlier. The aim of this lesson is to read which values each perspective puts first.

examples.title: An overall evaluation from two perspectives
body: Conditions (fictional): Two youth center programs in Haedeun are evaluated. The weights are efficiency 0.4, citizen participation 0.3, and equity 0.3. Program X has efficiency 80, participation 60, equity 70, and Program Y has efficiency 70, participation 85, equity 75.

Interpretation: With these weights, Y is ahead. If the weight on efficiency is raised to 0.8 and the others are set at 0.1 each, X $= 64 + 6 + 7 = 77$ and Y $= 56 + 8.5 + 7.5 = 72$, so the ranking flips.

pa-13.title: The Evolution of Personnel Systems: The Spoils System, the Merit System, and the Career Civil Service
explain: Who recruits civil servants, and by what standard, greatly affects whom government works for. Is it natural for the side that wins an election to install its own people, or is it right to recruit by examination scores so that they keep working even when the administration changes? The history of personnel administration is a process of seeking a balance between these two demands, that is, political responsiveness and expertise and neutrality.

The **spoils system** is a system in which the party that wins an election hands out public offices to its own supporters. In the United States it spread widely during the presidency of Jackson in 1829. It has advantages: it reflects a new government's policies quickly, prevents a particular class from monopolizing public office, and makes it easier to control administration through elections. The disadvantages are that civil servants are replaced en masse whenever the administration changes, so expertise and experience do not accumulate, and appointments easily drift into favoritism and corruption.

Criticism of the evils of the spoils system grew, and the death of President Garfield in 1881, shot by a man who wanted a public post, became the occasion for reform. The Pendleton Act was enacted in 1883, and the **merit system**, in which some positions were filled by competitive examination, began to take hold. The merit system appoints according to ability, qualifications, and results, and guarantees tenure. While fairness and expertise rise, excessive tenure protection can make government insensitive to policy change and rigid.

The **career civil service** is a system in which people make public office a lifelong occupation and build a career from lower to higher ranks. Its advantages are political neutrality, expertise, and administrative stability. There are the **closed type**, in which new recruits are mainly appointed to lower ranks and higher posts are filled by internal promotion, and the **open type**, in which needed positions are opened to outside experts. The closed type is stable but slow to respond to changes in the outside environment, and bureaucrats can harden into a single group. The open type raises expertise and competition but can be a burden on civil servants' morale and stability.

Many countries do not choose one but mix them. Political appointees such as ministers are appointed politically, and the great majority beneath them are career civil servants under the merit system. Some key positions may also be made open type. Where political appointment ends and neutral career civil service begins differs by country, and deciding it is a choice between political responsiveness and expertise.

The merit system also has limits. If selection centers on examination scores, more people from particular regions or classes may pass, and whether examination scores properly represent actual job ability is also debated. Representative bureaucracy, to be covered in the next lesson, arose from this concern. The systems in this lesson were explained centered on American history, so it should also be remembered that other countries' systems followed different paths.

Interpretation: Gap is ahead on the written test, but when combined Eul is 2 points higher. Even the same candidates change rank depending on the ratio, so how the selection criteria are set matters. The criteria should be disclosed and based on relevance to the job.

Step 2: Section chiefs and staff are career civil servants whose appointment and tenure are protected.

Interpretation: Political responsiveness is secured through political appointees, and administrative continuity and expertise are protected by career civil servants. Had all the section chiefs and staff been replaced as well, it would be closer to the spoils system.

pa-14.title: Representative Bureaucracy: Who Fills Public Offices?
explain: Even if a civil service examination is perfectly fair, what if the makeup of those who pass differs greatly from the makeup of society? If people from one region, gender, or class occupy most of the public offices and other groups are almost absent, the question arises whether policies might be made skewed toward that group's experience. **Representative bureaucracy** is a concept that came out of this question.

The core of this concept, put forward by Kingsley in 1944 in his study of the British bureaucracy, is that the composition of the public service should reflect the demographic composition of society. This is expected to let bureaucrats bring the values and experiences of diverse groups into policy decision-making and implementation, raising government's responsiveness and letting every citizen feel that the government is their own.

Representation is viewed in two ways. **Passive representation** is about how closely the proportions in the public service match the proportions in society, that is, a matter of numbers. **Active representation** is about whether bureaucrats actually speak for the interests of the group they belong to in the policy process. The assumption that passive representation leads to active representation relies on bureaucrats having internalized the values of their group of origin, and this link does not always hold.

Passive representation can be expressed simply as an index. $$R = \frac{\text{공무원 중 해당 집단 비율}}{\text{인구 중 해당 집단 비율}}$$ $R = 1$이면 비례하고, $R < 1$이면 과소 대표, $R > 1$이면 과대 대표다. 예를 들어 어떤 집단이 인구의 50%인데 공무원의 35%라면 $R = 0.7$이다. In English: if R = 1 the group is proportionally represented; if R < 1 it is underrepresented (과소 대표); if R > 1 it is overrepresented (과대 대표). For example, a group that is 50% of the population but 35% of civil servants has R = 0.7. (The index is R = the group's share among civil servants ÷ its share in the population; 공무원 중 해당 집단 비율 = share among civil servants, 인구 중 해당 집단 비율 = share in the population.)

Examples of turning this concept into institutions include policies that set targets for a particular group's entry into public service or select talent by region. Supporters see them as widening opportunities for groups that long had difficulty gaining access and as raising the legitimacy of government. Critics see them as possibly conflicting with the principle of selection by ability, and find it hard to set standards for which groups should be targets of representation. Also, because one person belongs to many groups, matching every group in proportion is practically impossible.

The limits can be summarized as follows. Even if the composition is right in numbers, if the group is concentrated only in lower ranks, its influence on policy decisions is small. Bureaucrats work according to the norms of the organization they belong to, so the evidence for the assumption that they speak for the interests of their group of origin is mixed. Representative bureaucracy is best understood not as a system opposed to the merit system but as a discussion aimed at complementing it.

body: Conditions (fictional): 40% of Naru's residents come from rural areas. Of 500 city hall staff, 150 come from rural areas.
Step 1: The share among staff is $150 \div 500 = 30$%.
Interpretation: Since $R < 1$, people of rural origin are underrepresented. However, this number alone does not tell us whether their views are reflected in policy (active representation).

Step 2: The shortfall is $120 - 90 = 30$ people.

Interpretation: If new hiring is 20 a year, it is hard to fill all at once and takes several years. How the target is set, the time frame, and harmony with other selection principles become the issues.

pa-15.title: Rank Classification and Position Classification
explain: How should civil servants be classified, and within what framework should pay and promotion be set? It can be based on a person's status and qualifications, or on the content of the work they do. These two branches are the **rank classification** (rank-in-person) system and the **position classification** (rank-in-position) system. Depending on which is put at the center, the methods of recruitment, assignment, pay, and training differ.

**Rank classification** divides ranks according to personal characteristics such as education, qualifications, and career, and sets promotion, pay, and authority by rank. It suits cultivating generalist administrators and rotating them among several departments, it makes organizational management flexible, and it can produce managers with a long-term outlook. On the other hand, job expertise is weak, and rank becomes status, so it tends to be closed. It is compatible with the status-centered career civil service.

**Position classification** classifies positions by the type of duties and their difficulty and responsibility. Because the content of the work comes first, it is easy to recruit specialists suited to the duties, and it fits well with job-based pay, in which the same duties receive the same pay. The disadvantages are that the framework of positions is rigid, making it hard to move people to other work, and that the classification must be revised whenever the work changes. It is unfavorable for cultivating generalist administrators.

The terms of position classification run from smaller to larger units as follows.
- **Position**: the duties and responsibilities assigned to one person.
- **Class**: a group of positions similar in type of duties and in difficulty and responsibility.
- **Series**: a group of classes similar in type of duties but different in difficulty and responsibility.
- **Occupational group**: a group of series similar in the nature of their duties.

To set pay by comparing duties, job evaluation, which expresses duties as points, is used. Points are given for factors such as responsibility, difficulty, and qualification requirements, and the summed job points multiplied by a unit price per point give the job-based pay. Even within the same class, the harder the duties, the higher the pay. In rank classification, those of the same rank and pay step receive similar pay even if their work differs.

In practice, no country uses only one. Countries with a strong rank classification tradition also introduce job analysis, and countries using position classification keep some rotating assignments and generalist administrators. Rank classification and position classification are ideal types, and real systems lie somewhere between the two poles. This lesson, too, is a theoretical explanation and not a guide to any particular civil service system.

examples.title: Job-based pay from job evaluation
body: Conditions (fictional): A position in Naru was evaluated at 40 points for responsibility, 35 for difficulty, and 20 for qualification requirements. The unit price per point is 30,000 won.
Step 1: The job points are $40 + 35 + 20 = 95$.
Step 2: The job-based pay is $95 \times 3 = 285$ (in units of 10,000 won, that is, 2.85 million won).

Interpretation: The harder the duties or the greater the responsibility, the higher the job-based pay. If the same position's responsibility score rose by just 5 points, the job-based pay would be $100 \times 3 = 300$ (in units of 10,000 won).

Step 1: The former approach leans toward rank classification, building broad experience around the person.
Step 2: The latter approach leans toward position classification, building expertise around the duties.
Interpretation: The former favors training managers, and the latter favors expertise. Conversely, the former is weak in expertise, and the latter makes it hard to move people to other work.

pa-16.title: Budget Reform I: Line-Item, Performance, and Planning Budgets
explain: Even for the same 10-billion-won budget document, one written as "personnel 4.0 billion, supplies 3.5 billion, facilities 2.5 billion" and one written as "road maintenance 6.0 billion, park management 4.0 billion" tell different stories. The former shows what the money is spent on, and the latter shows what work is being done. What a budget does changes depending on which information it is built around. Schick viewed the functions of the budget as divided into control, management, and planning.

**Line-item budgeting** (LIBS) sets amounts by object of expenditure (items such as personnel, supplies, and travel). Because one can check item by item where the money was spent, it is strong in accounting responsibility and **control**. But it is hard to know what programs the money is used for or how well they performed.

**Performance budgeting** (PBS) sets a work unit for each program (function) and determines the budget by multiplying the workload by the unit cost. It became known in the United States through the recommendation of the Hoover Commission in 1949. $$\text{예산} = \text{업무량} \times \text{단위 원가}$$ (That is, budget = workload × unit cost; 예산 = budget, 업무량 = workload, 단위 원가 = unit cost.) Because what the money is spent for becomes visible, it is useful for program **management**. But even though workload is measured, it is hard to reflect the quality or results of a program, and unit costs are also hard to calculate.

**Planning-programming-budgeting** (PPBS) links long-term plans, program plans, and the budget into one, starting from goals, analyzing alternatives (cost-benefit analysis and so on), and allocating resources accordingly. It was used at the U.S. Department of Defense in the 1960s and extended to the federal government. Its **planning** function, which links goals and resources, is strong. But it was criticized because goals are hard to express in numbers, it ignores the nature of the budget as political bargaining, and the data and work required for the analysis are so heavy that authority concentrates at the center. In the U.S. federal government it was not kept for long.

The three systems are compared as follows. LIBS focuses on inputs (items), PBS on workload and cost, and PPBS on goals and alternatives. In chronological order, LIBS came first, followed by PBS and PPBS. Each was a reform meant to correct the limits of the earlier system but produced new limits, leading to the next reform (zero-base budgeting).

One system has not completely replaced another. Real budget documents carry several kinds of information together. The line-item breakdown remains for control, and program information and performance information are often added on top of it. Rather than saying which system is better, it helps to ask which of control, management, and planning is most needed now.

examples.title: A performance budgeting calculation
body: Conditions (fictional): Haedeun carries out a road paving program. This year's planned workload is 25 km, and the unit cost is 120 million won per km (1.2 eok won).
Step 1: The budget is $25 \times 1.2 = 30$ eok won.
Step 2: If the unit cost rises to 1.5 eok won, it becomes $25 \times 1.5 = 37.5$ eok won.
Interpretation: The budget is explained by two factors, workload and cost. However, the quality of the paving and the satisfaction of users are not in this formula.

Step 1: In the item-based presentation, one can see where the money is spent but cannot see how much each program costs.
Step 2: In the program-based presentation, one can see that road maintenance spends 1.5 times park management, but cannot see the share of personnel costs.

Interpretation: The two presentations answer different questions. If the purpose is control, item-based information is useful; if the purpose is program management, program-based information is useful.

pa-17.title: Budget Reform II: Zero-Base Budgeting and Program Budgeting
explain: Many government budgets are set by "adding a little to last year's budget." This is incremental budgeting. It is stable and easy to negotiate, but once a program exists its budget continues even as its effect weakens, and new needs receive no share. The problem is that past decisions are treated as faits accomplis. The reform that questioned this practice is **zero-base budgeting**.

**Zero-base budgeting** (ZBB) does not take the previous year's budget as its baseline but has every program justified anew from zero. First, each department divides its programs into several **decision packages**. A package contains the purpose, cost, expected effect, and alternatives. Next, all the packages are ranked by priority, costs are accumulated and approved in rank order, and the process stops at the point where the limit of the available budget is exceeded. Only packages below the limit are reflected in the budget. This method began in private firms and was introduced in the U.S. government in the 1970s.

explain.alt: Five bars laid end to end horizontally with a cumulative cost scale (0, 30, 60, 90). From top to bottom, rank 1 security light replacement 12, rank 2 street cleaning 18, rank 3 library operation 15, rank 4 gymnasium construction 25, and rank 5 cultural events 20 continue to the right like steps. An orange dotted vertical line at the cumulative 60 position is labeled "budget limit 60." The unit is eok won.
explain.caption: Packages by rank and the budget limit

explain: The figure shows this procedure. The five packages are stacked in priority order, and packages from the one that pushes the cumulative cost past the dotted line (the limit of 60 eok won) onward are not approved. The cumulative total for ranks 1 to 3 is 45 eok won. Adding rank 4 brings it to 70 eok won, exceeding the limit. In this way the limit decides where to cut the programs lower in priority. If the limit rises, the cutting line moves down.

The advantages of zero-base budgeting are that it reviews outdated programs, has resources allocated by priority, and lets members of departments take part in the budget process. The disadvantages are that the paperwork is heavy and takes a long time, the criteria for ranking priorities can be arbitrary, and, because there are many hard-to-cut expenditures such as personnel costs and statutory mandatory expenses, it is difficult actually to start from zero. This is called the problem of rigid expenditures.

**Program budgeting** structures policy goals into programs and unit projects, shows the budget grouped by goal, and links it to performance information. It lets one see at a glance how much of the budget is spent on policy goals and what results each program produces. Its distinctive feature is that programs are grouped under goals rather than scattered by item, and it took in the strengths of performance budgeting and planning budgeting.

Real budgets are neither purely incremental nor purely zero-base. Usually it is a mixed method that takes the previous year as the baseline but re-examines programs in some areas. Because reviewing all programs every year is costly, there is also a method of reviewing them in rotation once every several years. Each method shows a trade-off among information, effort, and political stability.

examples.title: Cumulative cost of packages
body: Conditions (fictional): A department's packages in priority order are 8, 14, 20, 16, and 12 eok won. The budget limit is 50 eok won.
Step 1: The cumulative costs are 8, 22, 42, and 58 eok won.
Step 2: Through rank 3 the total is 42 eok won, within the limit, and adding rank 4 gives 58 eok won, over the limit.

Interpretation: What is approved is up to rank 3, a total of 42 eok won. Although 8 eok won remains under the limit, the lower-ranked rank 5 (12 eok won) does not get in. The remaining money becomes a matter of renegotiating the order of rank 4 and rank 5.

examples.title: Rigid expenditures and discretionary budget
body: Conditions (fictional): Naru's total budget is 20 billion won (200 eok won), of which 14 billion won (140 eok won) is statutory mandatory expenses and personnel costs.
Step 1: The budget that can be adjusted at discretion is $200 - 140 = 60$ eok won.

pa-18.title: Local Self-Government and Local Finance: Subsidiarity, the Tiebout Hypothesis, and Fiscal Independence
explain: Is it better for the central government to decide on street lamps, or for neighborhood residents to decide? The view that, because circumstances differ by region, it is better to decide close to the ground is opposed by the view that central coordination is needed to reduce gaps between regions. Local self-government is a system in which local affairs are handled by bodies elected by local residents, and underlying it is money, that is, **local finance**.

The **principle of subsidiarity** is the principle that matters should be handled at the smallest unit as close to citizens as possible, and the higher level of government supplements only what that unit cannot do. The basic unit comes first and the higher unit assists. This principle offers a standard for dividing authority, but judgment is required to decide which tasks a given unit can handle.

In 1956 Tiebout put forward a hypothesis explaining the efficiency of providing local public goods. If residents move to whichever of several local governments, each offering a different combination of taxes and services, they like best, the residents are **voting with their feet**, and local governments come to compete to attract residents. As a result, local public goods are supplied efficiently in line with residents' preferences. This conclusion relies on strict assumptions such as free movement of residents, sufficient information, a large number of local governments, and the absence of spillover effects between regions. In reality moving costs and limits on information are large, so the hypothesis is read as an idealized model rather than a description of reality.

Local government revenue sources are broadly of two kinds. **Own-source revenue** is money local governments collect themselves, such as local taxes and non-tax revenue, and **transfers** are the local allocation tax and national subsidies that the central government passes down. The local allocation tax is money given with few restrictions on use so as to reduce fiscal gaps between regions, and a subsidy is money designated for use on a particular program. This lesson uses simplified fictional definitions.

A representative indicator of a locality's ability to raise its own revenue is the **fiscal independence ratio**. $$\text{재정자립도} = \frac{\text{자체수입}}{\text{일반회계 세입}} \times 100$$ An indicator based on autonomous revenue, adding allocation tax with no restriction on use, is sometimes called the fiscal autonomy ratio. The higher it is, the greater the share of money the locality can spend on its own.

Dalbit City has own-source revenue of 1,200 and transfers of 800, totaling 2,000; Handeul City has own-source revenue of 450 and transfers of 1,050, totaling 1,500; and Bada County has own-source revenue of 200 and transfers of 600, totaling 800. The unit is eok won (100 million won).

explain: Look at the three local governments in the figure. Dalbit City has own-source revenue of 1,200 eok won out of a total of 2,000 eok won, so its fiscal independence ratio is 60%. Handeul City has 450 eok won out of 1,500 eok won, or 30%, and Bada County has 200 eok won out of 800 eok won, or 25%. The gap among the three reflects differences in the economic base from which local taxes can be collected. Transfers play a role in narrowing this gap, but there is also concern that growing dependence weakens a local government's incentive to expand its own revenue.

The fiscal independence ratio is a ratio of revenue composition, not an indicator that directly shows administrative efficiency or service level. There may be places with a low ratio that provide sufficient services thanks to allocation tax, and places with a high ratio that use their revenue inefficiently. Where to strike the balance between local responsibility and equity among regions is a value judgment, and this lesson does not settle on a single answer. It is an explanation of concepts using fictional cases and not an assessment of any real local finance.

examples.title: Fiscal independence ratio and fiscal autonomy ratio
body: Conditions (fictional): A city's general account revenue is 120 billion won (1,200 eok won), its own-source revenue is 36 billion won (360 eok won), and its local allocation tax (no restriction on use) is 30 billion won (300 eok won).
Step 1: The fiscal independence ratio is $360 \div 1200 \times 100 = 30$%.
Step 2: On the basis of autonomous revenue including allocation tax, it is $(360 + 300) \div 1200 \times 100 = 55$%.

Interpretation: The independence ratio is low at 30%, but including money that can be used without restriction it is 55%. Depending on which indicator is used, the same locality's finances look different.

Interpretation: This is a scene from the Tiebout hypothesis. However, this choice is not easy for households with high moving costs or little information, revealing the limit that the hypothesis does not hold for all residents.

pa-19.title: Integrated Problem Solving: From Policy Design to Evaluation
explain: The earlier lessons treated separately the tools of policy types, decision-making, implementation, evaluation, organization and personnel, budgeting, and local finance. A single real policy passes through all of them at once. Suppose Haedeun City begins a program called the "night safe walking route home" for alleys. We have to ask in turn: who will oppose it, how will alternatives be chosen, how will field staff handle the indicators, in what form will the budget be drawn up, and how will the effect be checked?

When solving an integrated problem, it helps to set an order of questions. (1) **Political terrain**: on whom are costs and benefits concentrated (Wilson)? (2) **Method of decision**: were the alternatives compared with the criteria and weights stated, or adjusted slightly from the current state (rational and incremental)? (3) **Implementation**: what behavior do street-level staff's discretion and performance indicators produce (Lipsky, creaming)? (4) **Organization and personnel**: who works, and by what standards (bureaucracy, merit system, representation)? (5) **Budget**: how are priorities set within the limit (zero-base, program)? (6) **Revenue source**: whose government's money is it (independence ratio, subsidiarity)? (7) **Evaluation**: how is the effect checked (difference-in-differences, internal validity)?

Each question is linked by numbers. An alternative's overall score is a weighted sum, budget approval stops where the cumulative cost in rank order exceeds the limit, the effect is found as the difference between the changes of the treatment and comparison groups, and the independence ratio is own-source revenue divided by revenue. Each calculation has assumptions. The weights are value judgments, priorities change with the criteria, and DID assumes parallel trends. One should not stop at finding the number but be able to say what assumptions that number stands on.

There are also questions whose answer is not settled as a single one even when the perspective changes. If Program A comes out ahead by the efficiency criterion and Program B by the equity criterion, which program is better? This question is not a matter of calculation but of the choice of criteria. The evaluator's job is to state the criteria first, show what data were used, and also say that the conclusion can differ depending on the criteria.

There are also common mistakes in integrated problems: asserting a policy's effect merely because an indicator improved (internal validity), missing that performance indicators change behavior in the field (creaming), accepting incremental practice uncritically (rigid expenditures), and applying one theory's explanation to every case. Each theory should be learned together with the conditions under which it fits well.

examples.title: From choosing an alternative to budget approval
body: Conditions (fictional): Haedeun compares three alternatives for the walking route program. The criteria and weights are safety effect 0.5, cost 0.3, and equity 0.2. The scores are 9, 5, 6 for Plan A, 7, 8, 7 for Plan B, and 6, 9, 7 for Plan C.

Step 2: Plan B, the highest, is chosen. Plan B's project cost packages in priority order are security lights 1.2 billion won, patrols 0.9 billion, an information app 1.4 billion, sidewalk maintenance 0.8 billion, and publicity 1.0 billion, and the limit is 4.0 billion won. The cumulative totals in eok won are 12, 21, 35, 43, 53, so up to rank 3 is approved, 35 eok won (3.5 billion won).

Interpretation: If the weights are changed to safety 0.3, cost 0.5, and equity 0.2, Plan A $= 2.7 + 2.5 + 1.2 = 6.4$, Plan B $= 2.1 + 4.0 + 1.4 = 7.5$, and Plan C $= 1.8 + 4.5 + 1.4 = 7.7$, so Plan C comes out ahead. Because the range approved is determined by the ranking and the limit, the criteria for setting the ranking must themselves be stated transparently.

examples.title: Effect estimation and cost
body: Conditions (fictional): In the district that ran the walking route program, the average monthly number of night-time reports went from 120 to 90, and in the comparison district from 100 to 85. The program cost is 270 million won (2.7 eok won).
Step 1: The change in the program district is $90 - 120 = -30$, and in the comparison district $85 - 100 = -15$. $\text{DID} = -30 - (-15) = -15$ reports.
Step 2: A decrease of 15 a month is $15 \times 12 = 180$ a year. The cost per report is $270000000 \div 180 = 1500000$ won.

Interpretation: Half of the 30-report decrease in the simple before-and-after comparison is a change common to both districts. However, the parallel trends assumption, and whether the number of reports represents the actual number of incidents, need to be checked.

pa-20.title: Bachelor's Capstone: Public Policy Design, Budgeting, and Evaluation Design
explain: In this capstone you design one policy in a fictional city from start to finish. The goal is to weave the tools learned earlier into one document and write it with a consistent logic from problem definition to evaluation design. This assignment is a learning exercise and is not a real policy proposal or advice for administrative practice. The city and the numbers are all fictional.

The framework of the design document is as follows. (1) **Problem definition and basis for the agenda**: whose problem is it, what is it, and why does government address it? (2) **Policy type and stakeholders**: predict support and opposition from Wilson's distribution of costs and benefits. (3) **Comparing and choosing alternatives**: state the criteria and weights and compare by weighted sum. (4) **Implementation system and risks of performance indicators**: consider who implements and what behavior the indicators will produce. (5) **Budget formulation and revenue source**: divide the program into packages, set priorities and the limit, and state whose government's revenue it is. (6) **Evaluation design and threats to validity**: state the comparison group, DID, the parallel trends assumption, and the threats. (7) **Limits and ethical check**: equity, transparency, other positions.

Let us look at a model composition. Haedeun designs "opening the library at night." The problem is that children of dual-income families lack a place to study in the evening. The benefits are concentrated on the families that use it and the costs are dispersed across all city taxpayers, so it has the character of client politics, and we anticipate the criticism that the benefits go to only a few. The alternatives are three: opening at night, creating small study spaces, and expanding after-school programs, and they are compared with the weights user convenience 0.5, cost 0.3, and equity 0.2, choosing night opening.

In implementation, we check the burden on night-shift staff and the problem of taking only the number of users as performance (the phenomenon of only easy-to-reach families increasing). The budget is divided into packages for extended opening hours, staffing, and safety management, and priorities and the limit are set. The revenue source is centered on the city's own-source revenue, and if some support from a higher level of government is assumed, its share and conditions are stated. For evaluation, the monthly number of uses at the opened library and at a comparison library that was not opened are compared before and after the program, and the effect is estimated by difference-in-differences.

We check internal validity and write down the design's weaknesses in advance. A local reading event held in the same period is a history threat, and if the opened library was originally a place where use was rising, that is a selection bias and parallel trends problem. Whether the number of uses represents learning outcomes is also a limit. Knowing these threats and then strengthening the design or lowering the strength of the conclusion makes for a good design.

There are three criteria for a good capstone document. First, the calculations are right and the assumptions are written down. Second, each step is linked to the previous one by logic (for example, the diagnosis of client politics leads to the weight on the equity criterion). Third, it does not hide other positions and limits. Policy always contains value judgments for which the answer is not settled as a single one.

examples.title: The numbers of the model composition
body: Conditions (fictional): The cost of opening the library at night is 180 million won (1.8 eok won) a year. The monthly number of uses at the opened library went from 3,000 to 3,900, and at the comparison library from 2,500 to 2,800.
Step 1: The opened library's change is $+900$, and the comparison library's is $+300$. $\text{DID} = 900 - 300 = 600$ (per month).
Step 2: The additional uses per year are $600 \times 12 = 7200$. The cost per use is $180000000 \div 7200 = 25000$ won.

Interpretation: A simple before-and-after comparison makes it look like an increase of 900 a month, but the effect is 600. Whether 25,000 won is a lot or a little must be judged together with other values such as learning outcomes.

examples.title: Finding flaws in a design
body: Conditions (fictional): One design compares only the number of users before and after the program, and in the same year the city held reading events at all of its libraries.
Step 1: A before-and-after comparison alone cannot distinguish the event's influence from the program's effect (a history threat).

Step 2: Since there is no comparison library at which the event was not held, DID cannot be used either. One must either take a library in another city that did not hold the event as the comparison group, or include in the conclusion a caveat that the event had an influence.
Interpretation: Finding threats at the design stage and then arranging a comparison group or lowering the strength of the conclusion is the honesty of evaluation.
